title: Best Dehumidifier for 4000 Sq Ft (2026): One Unit or Two?
h1: The Best Dehumidifiers for 4,000 Square Feet
dek: At 4,000 square feet, a single portable stops being the answer. Here's how to size it — and the whole-home and two-unit setups that actually work.
description: The best dehumidifier for 4,000 sq ft: whole-home units vs. two portables, what “4,500 sq ft” labels really mean, and sizing math for big homes and basements.
intro: Shopping for a **4,000 sq ft dehumidifier** is where the marketing and the math part ways. Plenty of portables promise to cover 4,500 square feet, yet a 4,000-square-foot home — or a basement that size — almost never behaves like one open, evenly damp room. Walls, doors, stairs and separate floors all limit how far one machine's dry air can travel.

So the real question isn't which box says “4,000” on it. It's whether you need a ducted whole-home unit, an installed basement unit or two well-placed portables. We worked through the same sizing math as our [dehumidifier size guide](/guides/dehumidifier-size-guide/), extended to larger spaces, and compared models on rated capacity, coverage claims, drainage and running costs.
topPicksLead: For a whole 4,000-square-foot house, the **Aprilaire E130** is the best choice; if you're drying one big floor or basement instead, a pair of **Midea Cube 50s** is the portable setup to beat.

Ducted into your HVAC, it dries upstairs bedrooms, the main floor and the basement evenly instead of leaving whichever room is farthest from a portable damp.

That headroom means it reaches your setpoint and cycles rather than running constantly through a muggy July. Our [best Aprilaire dehumidifier](/best/best-aprilaire-dehumidifier/) guide explains how it compares with the E080 and E100.

Installed in a basement, it can be ducted to the main floor later. See our [best permanent basement dehumidifier](/best/best-permanent-basement-dehumidifier/) picks for basement-only installs.

sections.heading: What size dehumidifier do you need for 4,000 sq ft?

blocks.text: Our size guide's chart tops out at “over 2,000 square feet,” because beyond that the answer stops being one bigger box. The practical method is to split 4,000 square feet into zones of roughly 2,000 square feet — usually one per floor, or one per end of a large basement — size each zone from the chart, and then decide whether to cover the zones with portables or one ducted system.

head: How damp is it?
Per 2,000 sq ft zone (DOE pints)
Two portables

rows: Very damp (condensation on walls, pipes, windows)

blocks.caption: Portables use DOE 2019 ratings; installed whole-home units use AHAM ratings. Don't compare the two numbers directly.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A 4,000-square-foot two-story home with 9-foot ceilings and a musty basement: the basement zone is very damp (40+ pints), and the size guide says to move up a tier for ceilings over 8 feet. That's a 50-pint unit downstairs and a 35- to 50-pint unit on the main floor — or one 100- to 130-pint ducted system for the whole house.

sections.heading: How we pick dehumidifiers for 4,000 sq ft

blocks.text: We don't lab-test. We compare current DOE 2019 ratings for portables and AHAM ratings for installed units, ENERGY STAR data, manufacturer coverage claims and manuals, and the CPSC recall database. Then we read owner reviews for patterns: units that can't keep up in large spaces, pumps that fail, sensors that read well off a separate hygrometer.

For this guide we weighted honest capacity for the space, continuous drainage (because two buckets is twice the chore), efficiency for long run times, and whether a unit can be monitored remotely when you're covering more than one floor.

sections.heading: What to look for in a 4,000 sq ft dehumidifier

items.label: Capacity per zone, not per house
items.text: A single portable dries the area it sits in. Count your zones first; that tells you how many units, or whether ducting makes more sense.

items.label: Continuous drainage
items.text: At this scale, buckets fill daily in summer. Choose a gravity hose to a drain, a built-in pump or a bucketless installed unit.

items.label: Efficiency you'll feel on the bill
items.text: Two units or one big one may run for hundreds of hours. ENERGY STAR, and Most Efficient where available, pays back here. Our [electricity guide](/guides/how-much-electricity-does-a-dehumidifier-use/) shows the math.

items.label: Remote monitoring
items.text: When units sit on different floors, a Wi-Fi app or a standalone [hygrometer](/best/best-hygrometer/) per zone saves you from walking the house to check.

items.label: Matching ratings
items.text: Compare DOE with DOE and AHAM with AHAM. Ignore saturation figures, which can be more than double the realistic number.

blocks.text: If every floor of a 4,000-square-foot home feels sticky in summer, a ducted system is worth the money — see our [best whole-house dehumidifier](/best/best-whole-house-dehumidifier/) guide. If the problem is mostly the basement plus one damp room, two portables cost far less and do the job. Smaller homes have their own guides: [2,000 sq ft](/best/best-dehumidifier-for-2000-sq-ft/) and [3,000 sq ft](/best/best-dehumidifier-for-3000-sq-ft/).

sections.heading: What “4,500 sq ft” and “5,000 sq ft” labels really mean

blocks.text: Search for a 4,500 sq ft dehumidifier and nearly every result is a 50-pint-class portable. Midea, hOmeLabs, Hisense and others all print 4,500 square feet on their 50-pint models. Those figures assume one open, moderately damp area with good airflow — not a house divided into rooms and floors, and not a basement with condensation on the walls.

items: **Same pints, different promises.** Two 50-pint units with the same DOE rating can claim very different coverage. The pint rating is the comparable number.
**Saturation headlines inflate further.** Some listings quote 100+ pints measured in hot, saturated air. Look for the DOE figure on the spec sheet or EnergyGuide label.
**5,000 sq ft is whole-home territory.** For 5,000 square feet of living space, plan on a ducted unit like the Aprilaire E130, or three portables covering three zones.

blocks.text: No single portable truly dries 4,000 square feet. For a whole house, the **Aprilaire E130** is the best fit, with the **Aprilaire E100** for tighter homes and large basements. If you're covering zones instead, buy two **Midea Cube 50s**, swap in the **Frigidaire FFAP5033W1** wherever you need a pump, and choose the **hOmeLabs 4,500 Sq Ft** pump model to keep a two-unit setup on budget. Then set every unit to 45–50% and check each zone with a hygrometer.

faqs.q: What size dehumidifier do I need for 4,000 square feet?
faqs.a: Split the space into zones of about 2,000 square feet and size each from the size guide's chart: 30+ pints (DOE) per zone if it's moderately damp, 40+ if very damp, 50+ if wet. For a whole house, that works out to about 100–130 pints (AHAM) in a ducted unit.

faqs.q: Is one dehumidifier enough for a 4,000 sq ft house?
faqs.a: One portable isn't, even if the box says 4,500 square feet, because walls and floors limit its reach. One ducted whole-house unit, such as the Aprilaire E130 or E100, can cover the whole home.

faqs.q: What is the best 4,500 sq ft dehumidifier?
faqs.a: Among portables marketed for 4,500 square feet, the Midea Cube 50 is our pick for efficiency and app control, and the hOmeLabs 4,500 Sq Ft model adds a pump for less. Just remember those claims assume one open, moderately damp space.

faqs.q: Is the Hisense 4,500 sq ft dehumidifier any good?
faqs.a: Hisense rates its 50-pint models for up to 4,500 square feet. The plain model reviews well; owners report sensor-fault codes more often on the pump version. Our [best Hisense dehumidifier](/best/best-hisense-dehumidifier/) guide covers the lineup.

faqs.q: What dehumidifier do I need for 5,000 square feet?
faqs.a: At 5,000 square feet, a ducted whole-home unit is the practical choice. The Aprilaire E130 is rated for up to about 7,400 square feet; the E100 for up to about 5,500, which suits a tight home in a moderate climate.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to run a dehumidifier for 4,000 sq ft?
faqs.a: ENERGY STAR lists the Midea Cube 50 at about 515 kWh a year, so two of them use roughly 1,030 kWh — about $170 a year at the US average of around 16.5 cents per kWh. Your climate and setpoint matter more than the brand.
